steps.title: In the ground
steps.text: Most copper sits in porphyry deposits: vast, low-grade bodies of copper-iron sulphide (chalcopyrite, CuFeS₂) strung along the Andes and the Pacific rim. Sediment-hosted beds, such as the Central African Copperbelt, come second. The two types supply about 80% of the world's copper.
steps.india: 0.2% of world reserves. Half the ore is in Rajasthan (Khetri), then Madhya Pradesh (Malanjkhand) and Jharkhand (Singhbhum).

steps.title: Mine
steps.text: Open pits are the main method: rock is drilled, blasted and hauled out by truck. Deeper ore bodies are worked underground. The ore is so lean that more than a hundred tonnes of it are dug for every tonne of copper.
steps.india: 23,000 tonnes in 2025, 0.1% of the world. Hindustan Copper works four underground mines and one open pit; its ore averages 0.77% copper.

steps.title: Concentrate
steps.text: At the mine, ore is crushed and ground to powder, then stirred with water, air and reagents. Copper sulphide grains cling to the bubbles and float off as froth; the waste rock sinks and goes to tailings. The dried concentrate is what ships to smelters.
steps.alt: Oxide ores take another road. Acid leaching, solvent extraction and electrowinning turn them straight into cathode: about 22% of mined copper.
steps.india: Smelters here run mostly on imported concentrate. Concentrate from Indian mines averages 23% copper.

steps.title: Smelt
steps.text: A furnace burns the concentrate in oxygen-enriched air. Iron leaves as slag and sulphur as gas, giving a molten matte of 50 to 70% copper. A converter then blows air through the matte until only blister copper is left.
out: Sulphur dioxide, captured as sulphuric acid

steps.title: Refine
steps.text: Blister is fire-refined and cast into anodes, which hang in a bath of acid. Electric current dissolves each anode and plates its copper onto a cathode sheet. Whatever is not copper stays behind, and the valuable part sinks to the cell floor as slime.
out: Anode slime: gold, silver, selenium, tellurium, platinum-group metals

steps.title: Shape
steps.text: Cathode is melted and cast into the shapes factories buy. Wire rod takes nearly two-thirds. The rest becomes tube, sheet, bar and foil, or is alloyed with zinc into brass and with tin into bronze.

steps.title: Use
steps.text: No metal except silver conducts electricity better, so copper ends up wherever power moves: wiring and plumbing in buildings, grid cables and transformers, motors, electronics and vehicles.

steps.title: Recycle
steps.text: Copper can be melted and reused without losing quality. Clean scrap goes straight back to the mills that make rod and tube; mixed scrap returns through the smelter and refinery.
